source: Cunha, Martins, Machado et al. (2017) A pig, an angel and a cactus walk into a blender: a descriptive approach to visual blending
finding: A coded visual blender (analogy mapping plus evolutionary search over part relations) re-produced most human-drawn blends and also made new ones.
numbers: 39 hand-drawn blends collected from 9 participants (14 cactus-angel, 12 cactus-pig, 13 pig-angel). Blender reproduced 23 of 39 (59%). Reasons given for 13 of the 16 misses: 2 impossible (inconsistent), 6 no such mapping from the Mapper, 5 because not all drawn parts were used in runs.
limits: Small N (9 drawers); three concept pairs only; coverage of human blends is the only validity test; no baseline system.
agent_relevance: A blend operator can be checked by coverage of human-made blends. Reporting why each miss happened is a good audit habit.

source: Cunha, Martins, Machado et al. (2017) A pig, an angel and a cactus walk into a blender: a descriptive approach to visual blending
finding: The search favoured blends that swap few parts. Fitness was the mean degree to which the relations of the base representation are respected.
numbers: Fitness f(b)=sum v(r_i(b))/#R(b), v in [0,1]. Mutation prob 0.05 per gene, recombination 0.2 per individual, tournament size 2. Authors say many more runs would be needed to reach blends with many exchanged parts.
limits: Random search biases toward blends close to one input; the 'optimality principle' was a single scalar, not a multi-criteria check.
agent_relevance: When an operator scores blends by one satisfaction fraction, it drifts to near-copies of one input. Add an explicit distance-from-inputs term in code.

source: Cunha, Martins, Machado et al. (2017) A pig, an angel and a cactus walk into a blender: a descriptive approach to visual blending
finding: Perception test: 'good' blends (prototypical parts clear) let people name both input concepts more often than 'bad' blends.
numbers: 30 participants, 12 blends (4 per pair: 2 good, 2 bad), each blend rated by 5 people; each person saw one good and one bad. Both inputs named correctly: pig-angel good 70% vs bad 10%; cactus-pig good 30% vs bad 0%; angel-cactus good 40% vs bad 10%. Neither input named: cactus-pig good 20% vs bad 50%; angel-pig good 10% vs bad 40%.
limits: Only 5 raters per blend, no inferential statistics; 'good' vs 'bad' set by the authors (fitness plus part legibility), so partly circular; bad blends always shown first.
agent_relevance: Unpacking test (can an observer recover both inputs) is a cheap acceptance test for a blend: ask a separate pass to name the sources without seeing them.

source: Pereira and Cardoso (Divago; described in Cunha et al. 2017 related-work section)
finding: Divago was one of the first systems built on blending theory. It used rules plus concept maps and a domain of instances drawn in a Logo-like language; tested on the house-boat blend with several instance sets.
numbers: Second-hand description only; no numbers. Ribeiro et al. (2003) reused Divago to make novel creatures, rendered as 3D OBJ files.
limits: Primary sources not opened (Pereira 2007 book; Martins, Pereira, Cardoso 2019 chapter, doi 10.1007/978-3-319-43610-4_5). Evaluation was by example, not a measured benchmark.
agent_relevance: Oldest design to copy: explicit input spaces, generic space, projection, fitness by optimality criteria. But no measured quality exists to justify copying it.

source: Cunha et al. (2017) related work on blend evaluation
finding: Evaluation of blend quality in computational systems is weak. Confalonieri et al. (2015) proposed Lakatosian argumentation to judge blends, but the paper says there is no evidence of an implementation.
numbers: Statement: 'there is no evidence of an implementation'. Steinbruck (2013) and Xiao and Linkola (2015, Vismantic) are described as example-driven, with no benchmark in this source.
limits: Second-hand summary of other authors' work.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a validated evaluation metric for blends exists. Use our own checks (unpacking, consistency, task fit).

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2019/2020, JETAI) A description logic framework for commonsense conceptual combination integrating typicality, probabilities and cognitive heuristics (TCL)
finding: TCL blends two concepts by generating consistent scenarios of inherited properties, ranked by probability, with a HEAD-over-MODIFIER heuristic to drop conflicts. It solves the pet-fish case only as a tied group, not a unique answer.
numbers: Pet fish: highest-probability scenarios (up to 20% in one setup, 35% in the other) are trivial or inconsistent; the first 43 blocks in one run are all inconsistent. The correct scenario sits at probability 0.138% (first setup) and 0.013% (harder setup) and is one of two valid scenarios left; TCL stays 'agnostic' between them.
limits: Formalism paper; authors say the machinery for getting probabilities from data is out of scope. Only toy knowledge bases (Pet, Fish, Athlete, Linda). Fails if the starting KB gives the highest probability to the property that should be dropped; authors state no formalization handles that case.
agent_relevance: A coded blend operator needs a human or a check to pick from the final tied set. Generating candidate blends is easy; selecting is the weak part.

source: Lieto and Pozzato (2019/2020, JETAI) A description logic framework for commonsense conceptual combination integrating typicality, probabilities and cognitive heuristics (TCL)
finding: Reasoning complexity of TCL equals the underlying logic (no extra cost for typicality plus probability). Applied to pet fish, Linda the bank teller, and creative recombination.
numbers: Authors state complexity stays that of ALC plus TR. Footnote: in creativity applications 'the final decision about what selection represents the most appropriate combination, is left to the human decision makers'.
limits: No empirical comparison to human judgments in this paper; evaluation is worked examples only.
agent_relevance: Typicality-weighted blending is tractable in a symbolic layer, but its quality is not measured against people. Design source, not validated.

source: Lieto (2019) Heterogeneous proxytypes extended
finding: Proxytype theory of concepts (prototypes, exemplars, theory-like parts used as needed) underlies the TCL line of work.
numbers: No blend-quality numbers in this paper; it is a theoretical integration paper.
limits: Theory only; no test of blending quality.
agent_relevance: Different representations for different tasks: choose prototype, exemplar or rule by task, in code.

source: Gomez-Ramirez, Herrera-Jaramillo, Geismann (2021) Artificial cognitively-inspired generation of the notion of topological group
finding: Formal blending as a colimit of two CASL specifications (continuous functions and groups), computed in the Heterogeneous Tool Set (HETS), re-derived topological groups in three ways. It is the COINVENT-style heir to Guhe et al. 2011 and the HDTP line.
numbers: Three artificial specifications produced; described as 'heuristic evidence'. No count of rejected or failed blends.
limits: Hand-chosen success case; no search over many input pairs; no independent novelty judgment; the known answer was the target (hindsight).
agent_relevance: A blend of two formal theories can be computed exactly by code (colimit), but the hard step, choosing which two theories and which generic space, was done by the authors.

source: Wang et al. (2023, CHI) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: GPT-3 pipeline: find connecting concepts between two domains (pop culture and a product), then retrieve or generate scenes. Three strategies: No-GPT, Half-GPT, Full-GPT.
numbers: 10 annotators. Accuracy of connecting concepts 56.0% / 55.3% / 58.7% across the three strategies; at least one of five connecting concepts good: 90.0% / 96.6% / 93.3%; overall 93.3% of pairs had at least one good concept.
limits: GPT-3-era model; five pop-culture domains and six products only; accuracy judged by 10 annotators.
agent_relevance: Roughly half of LLM-proposed bridges are bad, so a blend operator must generate several and filter. 'At least one good of five' is a usable acceptance rate.

source: Wang et al. (2023, CHI) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: GPT-3 facts about pop culture entities are unreliable by attribute type; made-up claims are the main failure.
numbers: Attribute accuracy overall 57% (mean 2.86 of 5); adjectives 79%, activities 58%, catchphrases 35%; inter-rater reliability 0.32 to 0.47. Scenes related to the connecting concept: at least one 98.3%; product scenes 89.1% vs pop-culture scenes 75.9% (raw 80.0% vs 63.4%).
limits: Low inter-rater reliability (0.32 to 0.47) means the measured accuracy is itself noisy.
agent_relevance: Generated 'facts' about an input must be checked against a source before they enter a blend (ties to G2 and G3).

source: Wang et al. (2023, CHI) PopBlends: strategies for conceptual blending with large language models
finding: Within-subject user study: PopBlends beat plain web search for ideating blends and cut workload.
numbers: 10 students, 6 blends each (3 baseline, 3 system). Ideas per pair 2.03 (SD 0.84) vs 0.87 (SD 0.56), Wilcoxon p<0.001. NASA-TLX mental demand 2.85 vs 5.80 (p=0.004), effort 3.05 vs 5.00 (p=0.006), frustration 1.65 vs 3.25 (p=0.026), temporal demand 3.00 vs 4.65 (p=0.028); physical demand n.s. (p=0.102). All 10 said PopBlends helped more.
limits: N=10, amateur designers; counts of ideas, not rated for quality; baseline was a free search engine; no quality check of the final blends.
agent_relevance: Idea count, not idea quality, improved. We cannot say blend quality improved.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models
finding: On a simile dataset, pretrained language models far out-predict ConceptNet at proposing the property that links two objects.
numbers: Table 3, P@10 / P@100 / P@1000, rows as printed (labels lost in text extraction): 1.12/2.70/5.90; 0.13/7.69/37.33; 1.59/15.72/53.08; 1.42/15.89/46.56; 2.59/24.84/66.38. Best row about 66% at top-1000. 66,442 property-object pairs; 96.34% of objects found in ConceptNet.
limits: Row labels are scrambled in the PDF text so which model is which is uncertain; precision at 10 is very low for all (about 0.1 to 2.6%), so top-ranked picks are poor; dataset is similes, not full blends.
agent_relevance: Language models are good at brainstorming many shared properties and poor at ranking the single best, so ranking must come from code and checks.

source: Ge and Parikh (2021) Visual conceptual blending with large-scale language and vision models
finding: Human preference study: CLIP-guided generators (BigSleep, DeepDaze) beat a text-to-image GAN (DF-GAN) at depicting a blend.
numbers: 20 blend descriptions (half model-written, half author-written); 6 questions tied to the unpacking, integration and general-quality principles; each answered by 9 unique Mechanical Turk subjects per pair per description. BigSleep preferred over DeepDaze; both over DF-GAN (exact percentages only in Figure 3).
limits: Exact percentages not in text; small description set; 2021 image models now obsolete; no test of model-written vs human-written descriptions.
agent_relevance: Optimality principles can be turned into 6 separate pairwise questions for a judge: a rubric scored in code.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Beyond pixels: visual metaphor transfer via schema-driven agentic reasoning
finding: A multi-agent LLM pipeline built on Conceptual Blending Theory (extract subject, carrier, relational invariant, violation point, emergent meaning; transfer to new subject; generate; diagnose and retry) beats direct image-editing prompts.
numbers: 126 metaphors. Human study: 100 participants (age 14-55, 45 male, 55 female), 45 images per method, 5-point scales; ours MR 4.47, MI 4.56, VA 4.51, VI 4.74, VQ 4.76 (Table 2 row). Good-Same-Bad: ours preferred over GPT-Image in 64.44%, Banana-pro 67.11%, Midjourney 72.89%, BAGEL 76.22% of pairs, judged inferior in under 10%. Cost: about 4 min 11 s and 8.3k tokens per sample; Generation and Diagnostic agents average 2.19 calls each (ideal 1).
limits: Gemini-3-pro is both pipeline model and one judge (GPT-5.2 and Claude-4.5 also judged); VLM-as-judge validity only in the supplement; authors' own benchmark and prompts; no independent replication.
agent_relevance: Closest recent evidence for a staged blend operator with an explicit schema and a retry loop after a diagnosed violation. Matches our state-machine view (diagnose, then revise).

source: Xu et al. (2026) Beyond pixels: visual metaphor transfer via schema-driven agentic reasoning
finding: Ablations: a strong single-shot prompt with the full CBT description recovers part of the gain over a simple prompt; the staged pipeline adds a further, smaller gain.
numbers: Gemini-3-pro judge, MC/AA/CI: Direct Prompt 8.79/8.03/7.63; Strong Prompt 9.02/8.13/7.68; the ablation rows are partly shifted in extraction, so the exact full-pipeline figures are not recorded. Largest gain on analogy appropriateness: 16.8% over the runner-up. Re-run with open models (Qwen, Qwen-VL, FLUX) said to keep the ordering with lower absolute scores.
limits: Gaps between prompt-only and the pipeline are small on a VLM scale that is near ceiling (8 to 9 of 10); no significance tests reported for the judge scores.
agent_relevance: The cheap part (a schema in the prompt) gives some of the gain; the pipeline adds more for extra calls. Test the single-prompt version first.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026 v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Large benchmark: blending is the hardest of association, analogy and blending, for both humans and 35 LLMs.
numbers: 35 LLMs; 75 humans (Prolific, 120 recruited, screened for AI use). Valid association 59.0% (LLM mean) vs 22.1% (human); valid analogy 53.4% vs 32.9%; valid blend 43.4% vs 12.8%. LLMs are 10-16 points better at association and analogy than blends. One model reaches 64.8% on blending but 55.4% on analogy.
limits: Entities random from Wikidata (>=78 sitelinks), so pairs are unrelated; judges are LLMs (3-judge panel; agree with humans 75% even when unanimous); humans had 5 items per task and skipped items scored zero, which lowers human scores; untrained humans.
agent_relevance: Blending is not solved by frontier LLMs: validity is under half on average. Never trust a model's own blend without a validity check.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026 v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Abstraction bottleneck: the failure is finding the shared (generic) space, not describing the blend once found.
numbers: Models find a valid generic space only 43.4% of the time on average; given a valid generic space they describe a coherent blended concept 97.1% of the time. Authors suggest missing experiential knowledge as one explanation.
limits: Explanation is speculative; judged by the same panel.
agent_relevance: Split the operator into two code-checked steps: (1) name a shared abstraction and check it, (2) only then build the blend. Step 1 is where models fail.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026 v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Inventive homogeneity: different LLMs invent the same properties for a blend, which breaks the independence assumption.
numbers: 19.9% (412/2,070) of invented concepts reuse at least two properties of another model's concept for the same item (cosine threshold 0.674, 99th percentile). Concepts invented by blending reuse at least one property 94.7% vs analogy 36.3%; two or more 37.3% vs 2.6% (14.3x). Same-family models 9.3% vs different-provider 4.1% (2.3x).
limits: Embedding-similarity threshold is a design choice; reuse could reflect genuinely obvious answers.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G4: samples from models give near-duplicate blends. Diversity must come from code (forced distinct generic spaces), not re-sampling.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026 v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Humans and LLMs occupy different parts of semantic space; ability rankings across the three tasks correlate across models.
numbers: Across 35 LLMs, association vs analogy performance r=0.71 (p<0.0001); analogy vs blending r=0.70; blending vs association r=0.54 (p<0.001). LLMs name more people and places and creation verbs; humans use more physical concepts.
limits: Correlation across models, not within a model over items; LLM judges.
agent_relevance: In a multi-person setting, human inputs add diversity the model lacks.

source: Schapiro et al. (2026 v6) Measuring combinatorial creativity in large language models and humans (KOMBINE)
finding: Related-work statement: no large-scale conceptual-blending benchmark for LLMs existed before this one; small studies by Wang et al. (2023) and Song et al. (2025). Song et al. reportedly found LLMs struggle to write noun phrases with emergent properties.
numbers: Statement only; Song et al. not opened.
limits: Relies on the authors' literature scan; Song et al. details unverified.
agent_relevance: The evidence gap is real: little is known about LLM blending, so our own test is warranted.

source: Hernandez et al. (2024, NeurIPS workshop) Alien recombination: exploring concept blends beyond human cognitive availability in visual art
finding: Two LLMs generate and rank concept combinations, using perplexity as a stand-in for human 'cognitive availability'; low-availability combinations gave images judged more novel than random sampling.
numbers: 150 output sequences per temperature level; a GPT-4 pairwise judge and ResNet-embedding similarity both rated Alien images more novel. No human raters.
limits: No human evaluation; GPT-4 judging novelty; ResNet embeddings also react to lighting and contrast; DALL-E gives in-distribution images; workshop paper; no quality (only novelty) measure.
agent_relevance: Novelty can be pushed by ranking low-probability combinations, but novelty is not value. Needs a separate validity check.

source: McCaig, DiPaola, Gabora (2016) Deep convolutional networks as models of generalization and blending within visual creativity
finding: Deep Dream and Deep Style are analysed as visual blending; neither keeps an explicit measure of novelty while generating, and high typicality (style imitation) trades off against novelty (Ritchie's criteria).
numbers: No quantitative evaluation; qualitative analysis. Repetition arises when the same inputs and settings are reused.
limits: Descriptive, no human study.
agent_relevance: A blend generator with no built-in novelty or validity measure will either copy a style or repeat itself. Add both measures in code.

source: Lu et al. (2025, CHI) Misty: UI prototyping through interactive conceptual blending
finding: An LLM turns an example UI and work-in-progress code into a blended UI under user-selected aspects; users saw mixed quality.
numbers: 14 frontend developers, 103 blending operations. Satisfaction mean 3.2/5 (median 3, SD 1.3); 31 of 103 below 3, 28 neutral, 44 above 3 (43%). Only 5 of 14 (35%) agreed the tool supports expressing their intent. Operation use: global blending 34.95%, drag-and-drop 33.98%, regenerate 18.5%, semantic diff 8.74%, code edit 3.88%.
limits: N=14, no control or baseline tool; self-reported satisfaction; authors state multimodal models cannot make perfect blends.
agent_relevance: Only 43% of single LLM blends satisfied; regenerate and diff were used in 27% of operations, so users needed retry and repair. Build retry and diff-based repair into the operator.

source: Cross-source synthesis of opened blending papers
finding: Across all opened computational-blending sources, evaluation is by example, a self-built metric or a small panel; no independent replication was found.
numbers: 0 independent replications found among 11 opened sources; 3 sources use only worked examples (TCL, topological group, McCaig et al.); user studies had N = 9, 10, 14, 30, 75 and 100.
limits: Absence of replication reflects this session only: search APIs (Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, WebSearch, DBLP) were rate-limited, so Guhe et al. 2011, Shrager, Eppe et al. 2018 and Martins et al. 2016 were NOT opened.
agent_relevance: Treat all computational-blending designs as unreplicated; use them as sources of operator structure, not proof that blending improves answers.

source: Wang et al. (2023) vs Schapiro et al. (2026): contrast on LLM blending
finding: An interactive tool improves human ideation (PopBlends) while a standalone benchmark shows LLM blend validity under 50% (KOMBINE). Both fit if the LLM proposes and a person or check filters.
numbers: PopBlends: 93.3% of pairs had at least one good connecting concept among five (GPT-3). KOMBINE: 43.4% valid blends per attempt on random entity pairs (35 LLMs).
limits: Different tasks, judges and model generations; not a direct contrast.
agent_relevance: Generate several and filter with code; this is what moves a 43% single-attempt rate to a usable rate. The step is untested by us.

source: Sato (2025) The way we prompt: conceptual blending, neural dynamics and prompt-induced transitions in LLMs
finding: Conceptual-blending theory is proposed as a lens for LLM behaviours (prompt-induced transitions and hallucinations), with mapping to attention and entropy dynamics. No measured results.
numbers: No experiment and no numbers in the opened text; repeatability across models is asserted, not shown.
limits: Conceptual essay; neuroscience analogies are not tests; largely self-cited.
agent_relevance: Do not use as evidence. Possible idea: watch token-entropy as an impasse signal; untested.
